Under the Bush and Obama administrations, drone strikes outside active war zones required high-level vetting, often demanding direct sign-off from the president or top White House aides.

The Trump administration expanded the CIA's authority to independently conduct covert drone strikes. This reversed an Obama-era effort to shift the majority of drone operations under the jurisdiction of the U.S. military for greater public accountability. The CIA’s drone program operates under Title 50 covert action authorities.

The DoD possesses its own independent authorities to conduct drone targeting. It executes drone strikes through the conventional military chain of command, primarily via the Joint Special Operations Command (JSOC).

The Obama administration had attempted to enforce a "unified" system where the CIA would find targets, but the DoD had to pull the trigger. This was done to ensure strikes fell under DoD's Title 10 military rules, making them subject to public casualty reporting.

But if the CIA and JSOC are operating in the same theater, they share intelligence and coordinate tracking data. 

Under Title 10, DoD commanders on the ground have the discretion to engage and neutralize enemy unmanned aerial systems (C-UAS). 

Operating under Title 50 covert actions, the CIA has the authority to protect its own covert operations and personnel. If an unknown drone compromises or threatens a CIA operation, the agency has the technical and legal authority to neutralize it.

In theory, neither agency is permitted to shoot down the other's aircraft. In practice, because CIA operations are highly classified and frequently unacknowledged, the DoD may not always know a CIA asset is in the area. This requires strict operational deconfliction (sharing flight paths and tracking data) to prevent the military from accidentally targeting a covert CIA drone.

Within the United States, federal law strictly limits who can disrupt or destroy an aircraft, as shooting down a drone normally violates federal aviation and signal interference laws. However, the Trump administration has aggressively pushed to expand domestic counter-drone powers:

• Under 10 U.S. Code § 130i, the Pentagon has the statutory authority to track and shoot down drones over "covered military facilities"—such as nuclear sites, missile bases, and designated installations. (3/31/2025)

• The CIA is statutorily prohibited from conducting domestic law enforcement or internal security functions. It has no authority to shoot down drones inside the United States, leaving domestic airspace defense entirely to the DoD, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the DOJ, and the FAA.

Because multiple federal agencies operate drones domestically (including the DoD, FBI, and Customs and Border Protection), decentralized authority has led to severe communication breakdowns.

In February 2026, a prominent example occurred when the DoD mistakenly used an anti-drone laser system to shoot down a U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) drone along the Texas border. The military incorrectly identified the government surveillance drone as a hostile cartel aircraft operating within military airspace.

The incident sparked intense congressional backlash, exposing a chaotic lack of communication between the FAA, the military, and homeland security agencies when operating counter-drone tech on American soil.

When the military or intelligence agencies intercept and down traditional unmanned aerial systems (UAS), they rely on a mix of "Soft Kill" (electronic/non-kinetic) and "Hard Kill" (physical/kinetic) weapons.

The military heavily invests in high-energy lasers (HEL) and high-powered microwave (HPM) systems. For example, the Pentagon's southern border task force successfully downed hostile drones using an AeroVironment non-kinetic system developed under the Army's Multipurpose High Energy Laser (AMP-HEL) program. Systems like Epirus's Leonidas use microwave pulses to fry a drone's internal electronics instantly.

Handheld or vehicle-mounted devices (like DroneGun or Titan) flood a drone’s command frequencies, cutting its connection to the operator or spoofing its GPS data to force an emergency landing.

Systems like the Raytheon Coyote use radar-guided, small counter-drone missiles or kamikaze drones to physically smash into targets. The military also utilizes automated rocket systems like L3Harris's VAMPIRE.

If an object is detected over "covered military installations" or sensitive airspace, North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) and the DoD have standing instructions to intercept.

Under Title 10 authorities, if an object fails to identify itself, disrupts military operations, or violates a Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR), the military has full clearance to utilize kinetic weapons or advanced directed energy to neutralize it.
